NVIDIA + World Labs turned 32 images into an explorable 3D world. 🚀 

World Labs’ Atlas took just 32 images of NVIDIA’s Voyager headquarters and turned them into a space you can actually explore.

Trained on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, Atlas uses the images as 3D spatial context to understand the building’s layout and generate new views in real time.

Move the camera.
Change your viewpoint.
Look around.

The crazy part?

Those new views weren’t directly captured in the original 32 images. 👀

This feels like a big step beyond AI that simply understands images.

We’re moving toward AI that can understand spaces, geometry, and perspective.

🤖 Robotics
🥽 Spatial computing
🎮 Virtual worlds
🏗️ Digital twins

32 images → an explorable world. 🌎

🚀 Google just open-sourced ARTEMIS 🌒.

It lets AI assistants control real Android phones like a human.

Think about that for a second.

You give the agent a task.

👉 It sees the screen
👉 Finds the right elements
👉 Taps, swipes and navigates
👉 Verifies what happened
👉 And reports the result

No need to hard-code every interaction.

And it connects directly to AI coding agents through MCP:

✓ Claude Code
✓ Codex
✓ Cursor
✓ Windsurf
✓ Antigravity
✓ VS Code and more

The benchmark numbers are interesting too:

⚡ 99%+ task completion on AndroidWorld
⚡ 100+ multi-step tasks
⚡ ~3–5 seconds per step with Flash mode
⚡ Multimodal targeting using accessibility, OCR and vision
⚡ Screenshots, execution traces and diagnostics
⚡ Python SDK for integrating it into your own test pipelines

But the bigger idea is what caught my attention:

Your phone can become an environment an AI agent can actually operate.

Imagine telling Codex:

«“Build the latest APK, install it, log in with a test account, test the checkout flow, look for unexpected popups and return screenshots of anything that fails.”»

And the agent actually drives the device.

This could push AI-powered QA, mobile testing, debugging and automation much further.

Google is basically giving AI agents hands for Android. 🤖📱

What would you build if your AI agent could control a real phone?

Google researchers are teaching AI agents to dream thousands of strategies before executing a single one. 🌙 🤖 

That’s the idea behind Dream-RSI, a new approach to recursive self-improvement from researchers at Google, Google DeepMind, the University of Maryland and University of Virginia.

The key insight is surprisingly simple:

👉 An AI agent’s history is already a simulator.

When an agent explores a problem, it creates a discovery tree containing previous decisions and their execution outcomes.

Instead of throwing that history away, Dream-RSI turns it into a replay simulator.

🧠 Generate thousands of alternative exploration policies
🌳 Replay them against previously discovered trees
⚡ Evaluate them with zero new executions
🏆 Deploy the best-performing policy
🔄 Explore the real world again
🌍 Add the new discovery tree to the simulator pool

Then repeat.

That creates a recursive loop where the exploration strategy itself improves from experience.

And the results are interesting:
• 2.43× fewer generations on VGG16 at comparable performance
• 1.79× fewer generations on LayerNorm
• 2.09× higher performance on ConvDiv at comparable budgets
• 1.44× higher performance on ConvMax
• Up to 162× fewer discovery-agent calls than SimpleTES on Lasso

The really interesting part?

Dream-RSI isn't simply feeding previous results back into the prompt.
It treats history as an executable search space.

The agent can ask:

“What if I had explored this differently?”

Without actually running all those alternatives.

One expensive exploration run can therefore become a simulator for thousands of alternative policies.

And every new deployment adds another “world” to the pool.

The AI doesn't just learn from what it did.

It learns how to explore better next time. 🧠🌳

NVIDIA is rethinking how we build AI agents in Python. 🤖

Instead of treating prompts, tools, state, callbacks, and workflows as separate abstractions, NOOA puts them into something developers already understand:

A Python object.
You define an agent like a normal class:
→ Fields = agent state
→ Methods = capabilities
→ Docstrings = prompts
→ Type annotations = contracts
→ ... = let the LLM implement the method

That last part is particularly interesting.

A normal Python method keeps its deterministic implementation.

But a method with ... becomes an LLM-driven agentic loop at runtime.

So the boundary between traditional software and agentic behavior becomes surprisingly simple.

And NOOA keeps the engineering workflow familiar:

🧠 Typed inputs and outputs
🔍 Built-in tracing of LLM calls, code execution, and method invocations
💻 Python-based testing, refactoring, and version control
🔌 Support for hosted and local models through LiteLLM

The bigger idea isn't just another agent framework.
It's treating agent behavior as software architecture rather than a collection of prompt and tool configurations.

That could make agents much easier to reason about, test, and compose.

One important caveat: NOOA can execute LLM-generated Python, so NVIDIA explicitly recommends OS-level sandboxing rather than relying on its in-process checks.

Would you prefer building agents this way, or do you think explicit tool/workflow abstractions are still the better approach?

Google DeepMind + Massachusetts Institute of Technology + Stanford University are letting AI regenerate software from design docs. 🤯🤖

What if code stopped being the source of truth?

Their new system, SMART, treats code as a disposable build artifact. 🔄

Instead, humans maintain natural-language design docs and AI agents regenerate the entire library from those docs. 🤖

The workflow:

→ 📝 Design docs become a dependency DAG
→ 🤖 AI agents implement each document
→ ♻️ The entire library is regenerated
→ 🧪 Generated code is validated against reference models
→ 🚀 Repeat

And the main branch contains almost no code.

The clever part?

The docs include worked examples showing step-by-step execution, intermediate values, shapes, and exact expected cost expressions.

So documentation becomes:
📚 Specification + 💡 examples + 🧪 tests.

SMART already spans ~50 design docs and ~9,000 lines of specification covering TPU topology, collective communication, schedulers, numerics, and frontier models.

A complete regeneration takes 1.5–3 hours and costs roughly $100.

The bigger idea is fascinating:

Humans maintain intent.
AI maintains implementation. 🚀

NVIDIA just found a way to make one LLM reuse another LLM’s memory. 🤖 🔄 🤖 

This could change how we think about LLM routing, prompt caching, and inference costs.

Today, KV caches are tied to the model that created them.

Switch to another model?

The new model can’t use that cache. It has to process the entire context again — adding latency and compute. ⚡

NVIDIA researchers treat this as a representation problem.

Instead of recomputing the context, they convert the source model’s KV cache into the representation expected by the target model.

And the surprising part:

No training required. 🧠

Their approach combines:

→ Closed-form linear mappings for each target layer/head
→ Cross-layer selection to find the most predictive source layers
→ RoPE removal and reapplication for position-independent mapping

For Qwen3 14B → 32B, a single source layer reconstructed 56% of the variance in target keys.

Using the best 8 source layers pushed that to 79%.

Across 6 model pairs from Qwen3, Llama 3.1, and Ministral 3:

4 retained 73–98% of standalone accuracy. 📈

And KV-cache conversion was 3–25× faster than processing the context again.

The bigger idea is fascinating:

What if an LLM could hand its computational memory to another LLM?

Models could potentially be routed dynamically based on:

→ 💰 Cost
→ 🧠 Capability
→ ⚡ Latency
→ 🌐 Availability

There are still limitations: tested transfers remain within model families, with matching KV dimensions, and dense full-attention models only.

But this is a compelling step toward portable model memory.

What happens when KV cache becomes portable?

🚀 What if you could re-film a video from a camera that was never there?🎬

Researchers at Westlake AGI Lab developed World in World to make this possible, using a frozen 14B video world model, without training or fine-tuning.

Give it a video.

Then give it a new camera path.

The system can re-film the same event from viewpoints that were never recorded.

🎥 Free-camera re-cinematography
⏸️ Bullet time
✏️ Video editing
🌎 Long-horizon exploration

The key idea is fascinating:
Source frames, depth/geometry, target-view projections and generated memories become visual evidence that is routed through the model’s native self-attention.

So the model isn't simply generating another video.

It's using its learned world knowledge to reason about what the scene should look like from somewhere else.

And it does this without training or fine-tuning the backbone.

This feels like an important shift:
Video generation → World exploration

Recorded video starts looking less like footage…
…and more like a navigable snapshot of the world. 🔥

🚀 Huawei is showing how diffusion models could become the visual backbone for robotics, 3D reconstruction, AR/VR, and Physical AI.

Marigold V2 shows how generative AI models can be repurposed for computer vision.

Researchers from HUAWEI Bayer Lab, EPFL, and the University of Bologna transform a pretrained diffusion transformer into a single-step dense prediction model.

The results are impressive:
⚡ 16–26% improvement in AbsRel over previous best results on KITTI and ETH3D
🎯 State-of-the-art zero-shot depth across 5 benchmarks
🔍 Preserves details like hair, fur, foliage, wires and railings
🖥️ Runs at 2048×2048 on a single 32 GB GPU
🧩 Uses 4-bit quantization + LoRA for efficient fine-tuning
But depth is only the beginning.

The same approach can produce:

👁️ See-through depth
📐 Surface normals
🎨 Albedo
📏 Metric depth completion

The inference pipeline is remarkably simple:

Just:
Image → VAE → Diffusion Transformer → VAE → Prediction

🔗 Code: https://lnkd.in/gamuzHpU
📄 Paper: https://lnkd.in/gTAaYMSN
